title: CPAs as purveyors of liberty and prosperity
primary_topics: Edited excerpt of the author's guest-speaker and inducting-officer remarks at the online PICPA national conference
The Confucian fisherman parable as the column's organizing image for the relationship between government, law, and entrepreneurial freedom
Comparative-political-economy survey (US, China, South Korea vs North Korea) used to argue that freedom + entrepreneurship + good governance produce prosperity
Articulation of the TATS framework (Transparency, Accountability, Truth, Sustainability) as the CPA's contribution to liberty and prosperity under the rule of law
The 160,000 PICPA members as a frontline economic profession positioned to be 'purveyors of liberty and prosperity'
sub_topics: Confucius adage 'give a man a fish... teach him to fish' as moral starting point
Five conditions of fisherman flourishing: skill, equipment (boat), freedom to sail, market access, plus protective minimal regulation
Tension acknowledged: occasional misjudgment, arrogance, greed, avarice as exceptions, not the rule
Government's role: guarantees and incentives; supporting institutions; minimal regulations against monopolization, hoarding, tax avoidance
US case: pioneers + inventors/entrepreneurs (Edison, Tesla, Ford, J.P. Morgan, Steve Jobs, Jeff Bezos) + leaders (FDR, Eisenhower, Biden) providing encouragement plus containing greed
China case: Mao's revolt; Deng Xiaoping → Xi Jinping leading economic transformation via 'One-Country-Two-Systems'; Chinese entrepreneurs (Jack Ma, Liu Qiangdong, Wang Wenyin)
South Korea vs North Korea contrast: private-initiative-driven recovery vs entrepreneurial-suppression and poverty
Universal claim: all peoples 'want, need, and deserve freedom and food, liberty, and prosperity'
TATS components defined: Transparency ('the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth'); Accountability of offices and officers; Truth in facts and figures and plain language; Sustainability
Conference theme paraphrase: 'transform society by embracing the possibilities and realizing the potentials of political liberty and economic prosperity under the rule of law'

TATS -- transparency, accountability, truth, and sustainability

institutions: Philippine Institute of Certified Public Accountants (PICPA)
People's Republic of China (as comparative case)
Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea)
Foundation for Liberty and Prosperity (FLP, implicit)

stances.claim: The goal of government and of law is to guarantee and incentivize entrepreneurial flourishing, build supporting institutions, and impose only minimal regulation against monopolization, hoarding, and tax avoidance — neither laissez-faire nor heavy-handed control.
stances.rhetorical_move: centrist-liberal political-economy creed via the fisherman parable
stances.evidence: Confucian adage + US/China/SK comparative case studies

stances.claim: Prosperity follows when entrepreneurial freedom is unleashed and contained by good governance, as exemplified by the US (Edison through Bezos) and China (Mao to Xi via Deng), while suppression of entrepreneurship produces North Korean-style poverty.
stances.evidence: Specific named entrepreneurs and leaders in each country; explicit contrast between SK and NK trajectories

stances.claim: CPAs, by characterizing their reports with TATS (Transparency, Accountability, Truth, Sustainability), become purveyors of liberty and prosperity under the rule of law and 'collaborators of Confucius and his fisherman, Edison, Morgan, Roosevelt, Jobs, Deng, Ma, and Liu.'
stances.rhetorical_move: professional-mission framing: integrates an entire profession into the FLP creed
stances.evidence: Definitional unpacking of each TATS component; conference-theme paraphrase

stances.claim: Despite different histories, traditions, cultures, ideologies, and mindsets, all peoples 'want, need, and deserve freedom and food, liberty, and prosperity' — a universalist anthropological claim.

notable_anecdotes: Use of the Confucian 'give a man a fish' adage as the column's extended organizing metaphor, expanded into a multi-step fisherman parable covering skill, equipment, freedom to sail, market access, and protective regulation.

Pairing of Edison, Tesla, Ford, J.P. Morgan, Steve Jobs, and Jeff Bezos with FDR, Eisenhower, and Biden as a compact theory of how American prosperity arose from entrepreneurship plus good-governance restraint.
Naming of Jack Ma, Liu Qiangdong, and Wang Wenyin as the Chinese counterparts to American entrepreneurs — a notable cross-civilizational pairing that anticipates later columns on China.
Coining (or canonization) of TATS — Transparency, Accountability, Truth, Sustainability — as the four-cornerstone framework for the accounting profession's contribution to liberty and prosperity.
target_audience: Business leaders, auditors, and financial officers
FLP donors and the FLP Scholars Society
Law and accountancy students studying professional ethics
Civic-minded readers interested in cross-civilizational political economy

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban shares an edited excerpt of the talk he delivered as guest speaker and inducting officer at the online PICPA national conference, where he was invited by PICPA president Marydith 'Dolly' Miguel of SGV & Co. He opens with the Confucian adage about teaching a man to fish and expands it into a parable about what it takes to save a fisherman from destitution: skill, equipment (a boat), freedom to sail the vast oceans, and market access -- and the role of government and law to provide guarantees and incentives, build supporting institutions, and impose minimal regulations against monopolization, hoarding, and tax avoidance. He surveys comparative political economy: the United States attained affluence through pioneers and inventors (Edison, Tesla, Ford, J.P. Morgan, Steve Jobs, Jeff Bezos) and great leaders (FDR, Eisenhower, Biden) who provided 'the encouragement to attain their dreams and the good governance to contain their greed and share their wealth'; China rose under Mao, then Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping with their 'One-Country-Two-Systems' philosophy and entrepreneurs like Jack Ma, Liu Qiangdong, and Wang Wenyin; South Korea rebuilt on private initiative while North Korea, despite technological and military bravado, wallows in poverty because of its grip on creativity. He concludes that the 160,000 PICPA members, by characterizing their reports with TATS -- Transparency, Accountability, Truth, Sustainability -- become purveyors of liberty and prosperity under the rule of law and 'collaborators of Confucius and his fisherman, Edison, Morgan, Roosevelt, Jobs, Deng, Ma, and Liu,' truly transforming society by embracing the possibilities and realizing the potentials of political liberty and economic prosperity under the rule of law.
